verdict.reasoning: Patient reports swelling on the left elbow for about a week: “I just noticed this, like, about a week ago or something… a weird swelling on my elbow… It’s the left elbow.”
Patient describes it as painless, warm, and fluid-like: “It’s not painful at all… it’s slightly warm, and I kind of feel like it’s a bit fluid inside.”

No trauma or prior episodes: “Have you banged that elbow? Did you have any kind of injury?” Patient: “No, not really. Not that I know of.” and later “Has this happened before?” Patient: “No, no, I haven’t noticed that before.”

History of osteoarthritis diagnosed by GP a few years ago: Patient: “I think I have something like osteoarthritis.” Doctor: “Has anyone ever told you that…?” Patient: “Yes, a few years ago.” and clarified as “A gp.”
No current medications: Doctor: “Are you on any medication on a regular basis?” Patient: “No, no.”
Ibuprofen recommendation given: “I would take ibuprofen regularly… 400 milligrams, three times a day… take that after food, not an empty stomach. If you get any heartburn, stop taking it.”
Peanut allergy documented: Patient: “I'M allergic to. To peanuts.”
No known drug allergies: Doctor: “Are you allergic to any medication?” Patient: “No, not that I know of.”
No known rheumatologic family history but unsure: Doctor asks about rheumatology diseases; Patient: “No. Well, I… think I have something like osteoarthritis… but in my family, I’m not sure.”
Desk job: Doctor: “In terms of your job, do you do anything physical?” Patient: “Not really, no. I just, you know, sit at the desk.”
Runs 2–3 times per week: Patient: “I do, I do do some sports. I run regularly. Like two, three times a week.”

Assessed as bursitis with mild warmth, minimal tenderness, low concern for septic arthritis: Doctor: “This seems like what we call the bursitis… inflammation of one of the fluid sacs around the joint.” Warmth and mild tenderness described earlier; Doctor: “it doesn’t look like to me that something called… septic arthritis.”
Osteoarthritis noted by history: Patient confirms prior GP diagnosis: “Yes, a few years ago.” Doctor clarifies type of clinician, indicating recognition as past medical history.
Peanut allergy is discussed but never explicitly listed as an assessment/diagnosis item; no statement in the transcript places it in the assessment section.

Doctor orders broad blood tests including inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatologic antibodies, and gout/urate, with forms mailed: “get some blood tests… check for inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies… and also check for things like gout as well… arrange some blood test forms to be sent out to your house.”

Transcript states results expected about 5–6 days from now (including form mailing and testing), not 5–6 days after the blood draw: “The time frame… the results will come back to us after about five, six days from now. It takes time for the forms to come out to you and if you get the test done straight away…”
Follow-up modality per patient preference: “the follow up appointment doesn’t have to be face to face… If it’s more convenient… over the phone… over video… That’s your call.”

Safety-net advice for worsening redness and pain: “if the elbow was to become very red, very painful, and the redness was to spread or become more intense, then you need to get on the phone or have a video appointment… as soon as possible because that would be an emergency.”
No plan to monitor osteoarthritis is discussed; osteoarthritis is only mentioned as past history without any explicit follow-up or monitoring plan.
Although peanut allergy is noted, there is no advice given in the transcript to avoid peanuts.

Video exam notes dry skin at elbow tip; swelling is implied by earlier description and visual exam: Doctor: “if you can just raise your elbow… then just bring it around… I noticed the skin was a bit dry on the tip of the elbow.” The entire visit centers on visible swelling of that elbow.
Elbow warmer than adjacent skin: Doctor asks, “Is it hot compared to the surrounding skin…?” Patient: “It’s a bit warm?” Doctor: “Yes, it’s a bit warmer.”
No tenderness at tip but mild adjacent tenderness: Doctor: “Is it very tender…?” Patient: “On the tip of the elbow? It’s okay. Just like next to it, like where the swelling is? It’s a bit…”
Fluctuant/fluid feel reported: Patient: “where the swelling is? It’s a bit. Yeah, it feels a bit fluid.”

Follow-up after labs via modality of patient’s choice: “you contact us after you’ve had the blood test done, and we can review things then… follow up appointment doesn’t have to be face to face… phone… video… That’s your call.”
